subtopic_detail: Late presentation with atypical timing and dehydration in a virilised infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department. A 24 day old infant labelled female at birth is brought in by parents with 3 days of poor feeding and 12 hours of persistent vomiting. Birth was at 39 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean; newborn screen results are pending. Parents describe an unusually enlarged clitoris that was noted by the midwife but attributed to birth trauma. Weight is 3.0 kg (birth 3.4 kg). The infant is drowsy with a sunken fontanelle. Bedside gas shows metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia. Blood glucose is low.

Your ED has no paediatric endocrinology cover; the tertiary team is on the phone.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 178, blood pressure 62/38, respiratory rate 54, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, apparently enlarged clitoris with partially fused labia, hyperpigmented genitalia
data_table.Bloods: sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 2.1 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32)
data_table.Access: peripheral IV secured, no central access

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV normal saline 20 mL per kg bolus with IV dextrose 2 mL per kg of 10 percent and IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat
options.rationale: Salt-losing CAH crisis needs volume with 0.9 percent saline (avoid hypotonic), IV glucose for hypoglycaemia, and IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat for the infant regardless of exact dose calculation while endocrine advice is sought; this is the RCH salt-losing crisis pathway. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Give IV 4 percent dextrose in quarter saline 20 mL per kg with fludrocortisone 100 micrograms orally and calcium gluconate for hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid worsens the hyponatraemia; oral fludrocortisone is too slow and unreliable in a vomiting infant; IV hydrocortisone provides the acute glucocorticoid plus mineralocorticoid activity needed at stress dose. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Correct hyponatraemia with 3 percent saline 3 mL per kg over 10 minutes as the immediate priority before other therapy
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or severe symptomatic hyponatraemia; in salt-losing crisis, volume replacement with 0.9 percent saline plus hydrocortisone corrects sodium physiologically without rapid rise and osmotic demyelination risk. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Give IV insulin 0.1 units per kg with 50 percent dextrose 1 mL per kg to shift potassium before adrenal steroid therapy
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose shift risks worsening the already-low glucose; hyperkalaemia in salt-losing CAH corrects with volume replacement plus hydrocortisone acting on the aldosterone-deficient state; insulin shift is a distraction and dangerous here. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

options.text: Await 17-hydroxyprogesterone result and the endocrinology team consult before giving any steroid therapy or bolus fluids
options.rationale: Waiting for 17-OHP results before treating a shocked hypoglycaemic infant with virilisation and salt-wasting picture would risk arrest; treat empirically and confirm biochemistry after resuscitation samples are drawn. (Source: RCH Melbourne CAH Guideline)

explanation.summary: Salt-losing congenital adrenal hyperplasia (usually 21-hydroxylase deficiency) classically presents around 1-3 weeks of life with vomiting, poor feeding, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypoglycaemia. Virilised external genitalia in a 46,XX infant may be missed or attributed to birth trauma. Newborn screening detects most but results are not always available at presentation. Immediate treatment is 0.9 percent saline for volume, IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and stress-dose IV hydrocortisone (25 mg in infants; 50 mg in children; 100 mg in adolescents) before biochemistry confirmation. Take pre-treatment blood for 17-OHP, cortisol, ACTH, renin, and electrolytes.
key_points: Salt-losing crisis: hypoNa, hyperK, hypoglycaemia, acidosis
Fluid: 0.9 percent saline bolus with dextrose; avoid hypotonic
Hydrocortisone 25 mg IV in infants stat (do not wait)
Draw pre-treatment 17-OHP, cortisol, ACTH, renin
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone at high dose has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity through renal glucocorticoid receptor spillover; fludrocortisone is added enterally for maintenance once absorption is reliable, not during crisis.

sources.label: Endocrine Society CAH Clinical Practice Guideline 2018

subtopic_detail: Painless bleed at 32 weeks with an unknown placental site
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an outer metropolitan hospital reviewing a 33 year old G3P2 at 32 plus 3 weeks who presents with a single episode of painless bright red vaginal bleeding of around 200 mL after intercourse 1 hour ago. She has no contractions and reports normal foetal movements. Her booking ultrasound at 20 weeks reported a low placenta but a follow-up scan was cancelled by the patient. Blood group is O positive and no antibodies. Her previous births were vaginal at term with no complications.

On arrival she is calm and haemodynamically stable and the CTG is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9
data_table.Abdominal examination: soft non-tender uterus, foetus longitudinal with cephalic presentation, no palpable contractions
data_table.CTG: baseline 140, moderate variability, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140 pregnancy), platelets 232 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 5.1 g/L, group and hold sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial assessment step?

options.text: Perform a gentle bimanual digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation before any imaging
options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated until placenta praevia has been excluded by ultrasound because it can precipitate torrential haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

options.text: Give a stat course of steroids with IV oxytocin infusion to induce labour and expedite delivery given the bleed
options.rationale: There is no indication for expedited delivery in a haemodynamically stable mother with reassuring CTG at 32 weeks before the placental site is defined; oxytocin risks massive haemorrhage if praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

options.text: Arrange transabdominal followed by transvaginal ultrasound to locate the placenta before any digital examination
options.rationale: Painless antepartum haemorrhage with a documented low placenta at 20 weeks and no repeat scan must be evaluated with ultrasound; transabdominal then transvaginal is safe with a well-defined technique and defines placenta praevia or accreta prior to any speculum or digital examination. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

options.text: Perform an urgent Kleihauer-Betke test and administer anti-D within the next 4 hours before proceeding to imaging
options.rationale: The mother is Rh D positive, so anti-D is not indicated; Kleihauer is used in Rh D negative women or for suspected large foeto-maternal haemorrhage volume estimation, not first-line here. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

options.text: Discharge home once bleeding stops as the CTG is reassuring and she has stable observations at present time
options.rationale: Even a small antepartum haemorrhage from suspected praevia can herald a larger sentinel bleed; admission for further imaging, steroids if praevia confirmed, and observation is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Painless antepartum haemorrhage in the third trimester requires placenta praevia to be excluded before any digital vaginal examination. Transabdominal ultrasound with transvaginal follow-up is safe and defines placental edge relative to the internal os. If praevia is confirmed at 32 weeks, admit, give a course of antenatal corticosteroids, cross-match blood, and plan elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks unless bleeding forces earlier delivery. Screen for placenta accreta spectrum in women with prior caesarean.
key_points: Painless APH: exclude praevia before digital examination
TAUS then TVUS is safe and accurate
Steroids for lung maturity 24 to less than 34 weeks
Anti-D if Rh D negative; Kleihauer to quantify large FMH
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG lower placental edge threshold for praevia is any placental tissue within 2 cm of the internal os on TVUS in the third trimester; edges 2-5 cm from os are termed low-lying and may allow vaginal birth after individualised review.

subtopic_detail: OGTT cut-offs at 24-28 weeks and treatment escalation
stem:
You are the antenatal registrar reviewing a 34 year old G2P1 at 27 plus 2 weeks in a suburban tertiary hospital antenatal clinic. She had gestational diabetes controlled with diet alone in her first pregnancy and delivered a 4.1 kg baby at term. Her booking BMI is 31. She has completed a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 4 days ago. She is otherwise well and taking pregnancy multivitamins and iodine. She has no known thyroid disease and no family history of type 1 diabetes.

Her capillary fasting sugar this morning was 4.9 mmol/L.

data_table.OGTT (75 g): fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (<10.0), 2 hour 8.1 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Ultrasound (26 weeks): estimated foetal weight 70th centile, normal liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure her the OGTT is within normal limits and no gestational diabetes intervention is required at this time
options.rationale: Fasting 5.4 mmol/L and 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L both exceed ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds for GDM; the diagnosis is made and further management is required. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and commence dietary review and 4 times daily self monitoring of blood glucose
options.rationale: ADIPS thresholds (fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5) diagnose GDM if any one is met or exceeded; first-line management is dietary modification with SMBG four times daily (fasting plus 1 or 2 hour postprandial), progressing to metformin or insulin if targets not met. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately as first-line pharmacotherapy for gestational diabetes
options.rationale: First-line is diet and exercise with SMBG; pharmacotherapy is added when 1 to 2 weeks of dietary modification fails to achieve fasting <5.0 and 1 hour postprandial <7.4 (or 2 hour <6.7). (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

options.text: Commence long acting insulin glargine 10 units nocte immediately given the previous large baby history and BMI
options.rationale: Insulin is added when dietary measures fail targets; jumping to insulin before a trial of diet plus SMBG is not the AU pathway even with risk factors for macrosomia. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

options.text: Repeat the 75 g OGTT at 32 weeks with random blood glucose in between to confirm diagnosis is accurate
options.rationale: A single OGTT meeting ADIPS thresholds diagnoses GDM; repeating the OGTT delays management and is not indicated. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

explanation.summary: Australian gestational diabetes diagnosis follows ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1 mmol/L or higher, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or higher, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or higher (any one). Management starts with dietitian-led carbohydrate distribution and glucose monitoring four times daily. Targets are fasting under 5.0, 1 hour postprandial under 7.4, or 2 hour under 6.7. Pharmacotherapy is added if targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks or if foetal macrosomia develops. Metformin and insulin are both first-line pharmacotherapy in Australian practice.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds diagnose GDM on any one abnormal value
Diet plus SMBG four times daily is first-line
Metformin or insulin added if fasting >=5.0 or 1 hour >=7.4
Universal 75 g OGTT screening at 24 to 28 weeks in AU
explanation.pearls: ADIPS uses a lower fasting cut-off than the WHO 1999 criteria (5.1 vs 7.0 mmol/L), yielding higher diagnostic rates; treatment reduces macrosomia and shoulder dystocia but effect on caesarean rate is modest.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic escalation after atony with a bleeding volume over 1.5 L
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 29 year old G1P1 who delivered a 4.0 kg male vaginally 25 minutes ago after a 90 minute second stage requiring vacuum assistance for maternal exhaustion. Estimated blood loss is 1.5 L and continues briskly. Bimanual compression is being maintained by the senior midwife. The placenta was delivered complete on the placenta tray. The uterus feels soft and boggy above the umbilicus. She has a history of essential hypertension on lifestyle measures only, controlled at booking.

IV oxytocin 10 units has been given and a further infusion is running.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Access: two large bore IVs, warm crystalloid running, cross-match sent
data_table.Uterine tone: soft, boggy above umbilicus despite bimanual compression
data_table.Prior medication: IV oxytocin 10 units bolus given, oxytocin infusion running at 40 mU/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic step?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 micrograms and repeat the dose in 15 minutes if the uterus remains atonic
options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disease because of severe hypertensive crisis risk; the RANZCOG PPH pathway skips ergometrine and moves to carboprost in hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device immediately as the second line uterotonic escalation therapy step
options.rationale: Balloon tamponade is an important step once uterotonics have failed but comes after the second uterotonic escalation; it is not the first response to persistent atony while carboprost remains an option. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: IM carboprost 250 micrograms and IV tranexamic acid 1 g with a second dose in 30 minutes if bleeding continues
options.rationale: With ergometrine relatively contraindicated in hypertension, next-line is IM carboprost 250 mcg (repeatable every 15 min to 2 mg total) plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g given within 3 hours; TXA reduces mortality per WOMAN trial. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Give sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms as the next line agent while awaiting theatre transfer arrangements
options.rationale: Misoprostol is used where injectable agents unavailable or as adjunct; carboprost is more potent and preferred where available with an IV in place, particularly with hypertension precluding ergometrine. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

options.text: Transfer to theatre immediately for hysterectomy given the ongoing bleeding despite the uterotonic given so far
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is the last resort after failed uterotonics, tamponade, brace suture, and interventional radiology; a second uterotonic and TXA are earlier steps in the escalation pathway. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony is managed with a stepwise combination of resuscitation and uterotonics. First-line is oxytocin (10 units IM or IV bolus plus infusion). Second-line depends on comorbidity: ergometrine 250 mcg IM/IV is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia; carboprost 250 mcg IM is the alternative and repeatable to 2 mg total; misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual is an adjunct where injectables are limited. IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours reduces bleeding-related mortality (WOMAN trial). Failure to control bleeding prompts intrauterine balloon tamponade, then brace sutures, uterine artery ligation or embolisation, and hysterectomy as last resort.
key_points: Oxytocin first, then carboprost if ergometrine contraindicated
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours in all cases
Escalate to tamponade, brace suture, embolisation, hysterectomy
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
explanation.pearls: Carboprost is a synthetic 15-methyl PGF2 alpha; contraindicated in active asthma because of bronchospasm risk; requires refrigeration; peak effect within 20 minutes.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27 year old G1P0 at 30 plus 4 weeks who was admitted 4 days ago after confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. She has completed a course of betamethasone and is on oral erythromycin. Today she reports mild lower abdominal discomfort intermittently and offensive smelling liquor since this morning. Foetal movements are reduced compared to yesterday. She has no vaginal bleeding.

Her temperature has risen this shift; the midwife has just recorded a further rise now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4, foetal heart rate 172
data_table.Abdomen: uterus soft, palpable irregular contractions 1 in 10 minutes with mild tenderness
data_table.CTG: baseline 172, minimal variability, no decelerations, no accelerations for 30 minutes
data_table.Bloods: white cell count 18.6 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0 pregnancy), CRP 84 mg/L (<5), lactate 2.6 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Continue oral erythromycin, hydrate with IV fluid, and add IV paracetamol with reassessment in 4 hours
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia (maternal and foetal), raised inflammatory markers, uterine tenderness, and offensive liquor meet clinical chorioamnionitis criteria; oral macrolide alone is inadequate and delaying delivery risks maternal sepsis and foetal death. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.text: Commence IV broad spectrum antibiotics and expedite delivery with neonatal team standby for the delivery event
options.rationale: Clinical chorioamnionitis mandates IV broad spectrum antibiotics (typical AU regimen ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole) and expedited delivery irrespective of gestation because ongoing infection worsens neonatal and maternal outcomes; neonatal team standby is essential at 30 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.text: Give a second course of betamethasone and plan tocolysis with nifedipine to reach 32 weeks before delivery is planned
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in chorioamnionitis; a second course of steroids is not appropriate when the priority is delivery to reduce maternal and foetal harm from ongoing sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.text: Perform an urgent amniocentesis to obtain amniotic fluid culture before deciding on delivery timing today
options.rationale: Amniocentesis in overt clinical chorioamnionitis delays definitive management; clinical criteria are sufficient to start antibiotics and expedite delivery without waiting for culture. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.text: Discharge home with oral amoxicillin and clindamycin and daily antenatal review until 34 weeks completed for delivery
options.rationale: Discharge with oral antibiotics is unsafe in overt chorioamnionitis; the patient requires IV antibiotics and delivery in a facility with neonatal intensive care support. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

explanation.summary: Clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed by maternal fever plus at least two of maternal tachycardia, foetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, and maternal leukocytosis. Management is IV broad spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin plus gentamicin, adding metronidazole or clindamycin for anaerobic cover post-caesarean) and expedited delivery regardless of gestation because expectant management increases neonatal sepsis, cerebral palsy, and maternal septic shock. Tocolysis is contraindicated. Vaginal birth is preferred unless obstetric indications require caesarean.
key_points: Fever plus two of: mat/fetal tachycardia, tender uterus, offensive liquor, leukocytosis
IV amp + gentamicin + metronidazole is typical AU regimen
Expedite delivery; do not tocolyse
Neonatal team standby for early onset sepsis
explanation.pearls: The ORACLE II arm found erythromycin (not co-amoxiclav) reduces neonatal composite morbidity in PPROM without chorioamnionitis; co-amoxiclav in PPROM increased necrotising enterocolitis so amoxicillin plus clavulanate is avoided in this setting.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

subtopic: Pre-eclampsia superimposed on chronic kidney disease
subtopic_detail: Diagnosis when baseline proteinuria confounds standard cut-offs
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 35 year old G2P1 at 33 plus 2 weeks with known IgA nephropathy and baseline proteinuria of around 500 mg per 24 hours pre-pregnancy on losartan (ceased pre-pregnancy). Her booking BP was 128/82. Today her BP is repeatedly 156/104 and she reports 2 days of frontal headache and blurring on the peripheries of vision. She has right upper quadrant discomfort and mild ankle swelling. Her creatinine baseline was 92 micromol/L pre-pregnancy.

Her partner has cared for their first child at home and asks whether she must stay in hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 158/104 (repeated 156/102), respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8, foetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140), platelets 122 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 118 micromol/L (baseline 92), ALT 68 U/L (<40), urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.36)
data_table.Urine: protein-to-creatinine ratio 92 mg/mmol (baseline 55, threshold for pre-eclampsia >30)
data_table.Foetal: estimated foetal weight 15th centile, growth crossing centiles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Give a course of steroids for foetal lung maturity and defer delivery until 37 weeks to reach term status
options.rationale: Steroids are appropriate but deferring delivery to 37 weeks with severe features (visual symptoms, thrombocytopenia, LFT derangement, growth restriction) risks eclampsia, HELLP progression, and placental abruption; delivery is timely after stabilisation, typically within 24-48 hours. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Restart losartan for baseline renal protection alongside oral labetalol 200 mg twice daily and outpatient BP diary
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated in pregnancy because of foetotoxicity (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios); outpatient management is unsafe with severe features. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Give oral prazosin 500 micrograms three times daily as blood pressure control while continuing routine antenatal visits
options.rationale: Prazosin is a second or third-line antihypertensive in pregnancy; severe pre-eclampsia with cerebral symptoms needs immediate parenteral or oral rapid-acting therapy (labetalol IV or nifedipine IR) and admission, not outpatient escalation. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Discharge home with 4 hourly self BP monitoring and daily foetal movements diary and specialist review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Discharging severe hypertension with cerebral symptoms and foetal growth restriction is unsafe; the risk of eclampsia, stroke, and placental abruption mandates admission. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Admit for oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate release, IV magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, and delivery planning
options.rationale: Severe hypertension with cerebral symptoms, thrombocytopenia trend, rising creatinine above baseline, raised ALT, foetal growth restriction, and proteinuria more than doubled from baseline meets superimposed pre-eclampsia with severe features; treatment is BP control (labetalol or nifedipine IR), magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/h, and delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Superimposed pre-eclampsia on chronic hypertension or chronic kidney disease is diagnosed when new severe hypertension emerges after 20 weeks with new organ dysfunction (thrombocytopenia under 150, creatinine above baseline, ALT/AST above 2x normal, cerebral or visual symptoms, pulmonary oedema) or a doubling of the baseline proteinuria plus new organ dysfunction. Severe features mandate admission, BP control with oral nifedipine IR, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine, IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (4 g loading dose over 20 min then 1 g per hour), and timely delivery. Antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity are appropriate 24 to less than 34 weeks.
key_points: Superimposed pre-eclampsia: new organ dysfunction on chronic HTN/CKD
Treat severe HTN: nifedipine IR, labetalol IV, hydralazine IV
MgSO4 4 g load then 1 g/h for seizure prophylaxis
ACE inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: MgSO4 toxicity signs: loss of patellar reflex (first), respiratory depression, then cardiac; calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent solution IV is the antidote; monitor reflexes, respirations, and urine output rather than levels in most units.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines Hypertension in Pregnancy
